p: Yeah, the diversion rate is certainly higher in the Upper West Side than it is in Hunts Point at this moment, and that's something.

So because if we're doing it based on density, you know, I would consider the Upper West Side very dense, and so just trying to understand what– if there are any things that we can see based on the differences given the density seems to be kind of similar.

Yeah. And I think that's something that in our last waste

characterization study, which came out— 2023. Okay. I don't remember exactly what—, when that was, but I remember working on it. One of the things that we looked at was sort of the stratification by both density and by median household income in the districts that we were sorting the waste from. It's something that– I don't have the details in front of me, but I'm happy to go into detail with you at a later date. And as we look to the next waste characterization study for residential waste, which I think is required by '28, we will certainly continue that work and see if anything's changed since 23. Hopefully things have, but you know, I would love to, to work with you on how to increase diversion. In, in your neighborhood.
Thank you. And speaking of Council Member Brewer, I will turn it over.

Thank you very much. I have lots of questions. First of all, I want to say thank you to a rock star. His name is James Lederer [sp?]. And then also want to thank Superintendent Baldwin because he's great. And I had to deal with the East Side transfer station when I

was borough president. That was hell. So I just want to say we did it.
We were there together.

So anyway, service— I just have a question. One of the problems–, I call it service substitution. I know that also, I want to thank you for mentioning the Solid Waste Advisory Boards. I worked hard to get Manhattan to be as strong as it is now when I was borough president, and they are doing a great job. One of the problems is that I think if you could switch from more organics collection and then pick what you wanna do less of, be it recycling or something else. One of the problems is that the buildings, the large ones that are not complying, complain they have to keep the organics too long. Can you think about switching so you have organics— I'm making this up— two or tree times and then recycling or something else less? Have you thought about that?
So I wouldn't want to decrease the frequency of recycling collection.
Whatever. I mean, pick something.
because it's, it's already just once a week—
[interposing] But organics needs to be picked up more often. Is that something that you're considering?
It's something that we can certainly take a look at that would require additional resources to do. So, but it's something that we're happy to take a look at.

Okay. Because I think one of the problems is they keep it too long and then they complain in the buildings that it's causing a problem. So that would be something to think about. Second is when you do your education efforts, do you go for those that are persistently low participation? Is that where you focus? How do you focus where you're going to do your education? Picking up on some of the earlier questions.

Yeah, absolutely. We do focus our education on places that have lower diversion rates. We also, in the past, have done targeted education and outreach to buildings that

have received multiple enforcement violations for failure to recycle or failure to compost. I think that's something that we'd like to stand up again, particularly as we are looking to expand the participation in the composting program.

In terms of schools, I don't— maybe– I listened to your testimony on the cell phone. I don't think you mentioned the schools. How is their rate doing? In the past, what we would do is give certificates to those schools that are doing well because they do need some kind of support. It's not easy to do– low staff numbers, low pay for the kitchen staff, etcetera. I work with all my schools trying to make sure that they do it, but it doesn't always happen. How are you working with the schools?

Yeah, so we work very closely with the schools, both to train the building staff, the staff in kitchens and the porters that actually collect the trash, as well as the teachers that are educating the kids, and provide programming for the kids that are learning in schools themselves. So it's a two-pronged effort. I think it's something that we can certainly spend more time

on. I would like to bring back some of the programs from the past that focused on really celebrating the wins and celebrating schools that have done—

[interposing] Could you get back to the committee the data on schools that are doing well, schools that are not, and that kind of information? My understanding is there's low on staffing in the kitchen for obvious reasons, and recycling goes out the door. I'm just— that's my experience. So I'd love to see the numbers.
Yeah, we can provide you whatever we have.
Okay. Rikers Island, if it closes, which I hope it does, what four waste treatment plants will close to be able to have a brand new one there? Do you know which ones? My understanding is it's four.
I think you're referring to wastewater treatment plants.
I am, yeah. But not— I know that's the DEP and not you, but do you have any import— into that at all?
I don't. And, you know, we would love to see a composting facility on record.
That's what I'm saying. Could you also— that would be something that you would consider?
Absolutely.
Okay.
Yeah.
And then in terms of NYCHA, that's an issue. How are you dealing with NYCHA? It's an ongoing issue. The chutes are small. I know the issues. What is the— what are you doing with NYCHA?

Yeah, so we are— we continue to engage with NYCHA. Obviously there have been challenges around waste management at NYCHA for many, many decades now, and we haven't found a sort of great set of solutions to be able to solve all of them at the same time. But we work with NYCHA on a regular basis. I think first and foremost to make sure that we are keeping– or that we and they are keeping the developments clean.
Do you have any pilots that are working with NYCHA?
We've done several pilots in the past with NYCHA. Kate or Jen, do you want to–
[interposing] Usually it's just going door to door with residents. That's not necessarily sustainable.

Hi, Council Member. Yes, NYCHA was very engaged in the development of the draft Solid Waste Management Plan. They're one of the stakeholder groups that's contributed to specific initiatives, and we do have some particular things we commit to working with them over time. They've been particularly innovative with a mattress recycling pilot that we have stayed in touch with them about and are considering expanding.
I see mattresses on the street, but okay.

Yeah, these are from the developments. They've also done a lot with redesigning their waste yards to look at how can they collect recyclables separately that links in with the diversion rate. So areas where they

consolidate waste on their different campuses. And one of the things they've focused on, to the Commissioner's point, is the paper stream and how do they really extract the paper and cardboard that has value to the city. So we'll continue to work with them on all of those things.
Could we get some data on NYCHA also, again, back to the committee?
Certainly. And we also include some specifics on them in our biennial reports on the SWMP that are posted on the DSNY website.
Okay, thank you.

Thank you, Council Member Brewer. I just want to continue piggybacking off of first on NYCHA and then into organics. So one in 17 New Yorkers live in NYCHA, and I'm curious to know what is the buy-in, or if you have that data specifically diversion rates on NYCHA properties and NYCHA campuses as compared to the rest of the city.

Yeah, we don't have that data specifically for NYCHA because they're collected on this— on the same household routes that collect the surrounding neighborhoods. But I would

say, to the point you were making earlier, that parts of the city that have higher concentration of NYCHA developments tend to have lower diversion rates. I'm not saying that's because of NYCHA, but that is a correlation there. We have studied NYCHA waste in the past. I think one of our prior waste characterization studies included a subsort for NYCHA, and, you know, I think there are— I'm not going to beat around the bush— there are some very real challenges around waste management generally. And, you know, our priority with NYCHA is keeping their facilities clean and having them be places that, you know, really support the residents that live there. I think we should also focus on recycling, but keeping developments clean is our number one priority.
And when you say keeping developments clean, can you just elaborate what that means from the DSNY standpoint when it comes to NYCHA?

Yeah, I think just making sure that residents understand how and where to put out their trash and are doing so properly. In the past, there have been a lot of issues with people just not knowing how to do it. As

Councilmember Brewer mentioned, a lot of the chutes are like this big. You can't fit anything in a chute that big. And so then people are forced to bring their trash bags downstairs. Do they put them by the door? Do they put them by the fire hydrant on the street? I think NYCHA has done a much better job now of being very specific with residents about what to do with the trash that doesn't fit in the chute, what to do if the chute's broken, which happens pretty frequently. And so I think that's gotten better, and that has been for the past few years where we have focused a lot of our efforts is being very clear about documenting and educating residents around what the proper waste management practices are, and then working with NYCHA staff and sanitation workers to make sure that that's being implemented across the board.

So I want to be clear that the– you know, I am a fan of composting and organics. However, when you're looking at situations like NYCHA where you see, or the city in general, where you're seeing diversion rates with recycling are going down year after year after year after year, I'm curious why organics waste and– the

organics waste diversion such a priority for the admin, when our recycling diversion rates are abysmal?

So I don't think our recycling diversion rates are abysmal. We're capturing around 50 percent of the material that could be recycled on any given day. The reason that we're focused on organics diversion is because our capture rate on organics, which is a program that has been in effect for a much shorter period of time, is much lower. We are not capturing nearly 50 percent right now. We think that we can get some really substantial increases in both participation capture and diversion in, you know, short order. And so that's where we're focused. There's also, just from the perspective of the climate and greenhouse gas emissions, that's really where the largest impact is of the waste stream on greenhouse gas emissions is in organic waste. And so if we can maximize diversion there, we can have a greater impact on reducing climate change.

You said— I just want to make sure that I have the data properly. You say that we're capturing 50 percent of our diversion,

but on the revised draft SWMP, the waste projections on Table ES9, it says that our diversion rate, if we stick to business as usual, will be 19.6 percent of DSNY managed waste, but if we implement the proposed programs, it'll be 20.6 percent. But you're saying that we have 50 percent diversion rate. Can you explain for everyone that might be looking at this what— where the difference is, where it comes from, and how we can—

Yeah, so the difference is that I was referring to the capture rate. So that's specifically for designated recyclable materials, things like comingled paper, cardboard in one stream, and then metal, glass, plastic, and containers and cartons in the other stream. Those materials together make up 32-33 percent of all of the waste stream. When we look at just that 32 or 33 percent, we are capturing about— it's usually just under 50 percent of that share. And so 50 percent of 33 percent, roughly 16.5 percent, that's the sort of traditional recyclable share of our overall diversion rate.
Great. So you see, everyone, they're not lying to you. The math works. Okay, going into—
[interposing] we'll have to do like a whiteboard explainer video.

Yes, please. I'm happy to pull it out. So according to the 2023 Waste Characterization Study, approximately a third of residential waste is organic matter, suitable suitable for composting. What resources would the department need to divert all organic waste from landfills and incinerators? Is there a specific– is there a need for specific facilities, authority, or staffing resources?

So I think the number one thing that we need is New Yorkers to participate, and that's where our focus is right now, is increasing participation, increasing diversion, and getting more collected material. We have at this moment processing capacity for substantially more material than we currently collect, so that is not a constraint on us at this moment. If we were to collect 100 percent of the organics that are out there in the waste stream, we would obviously need

more capacity, and that's where facilities like a potential future Rikers compost facility would come in. And as we have the good problem of New Yorkers separating too much organic waste, we will work with City Council on identifying where and how to build those facilities.
What are the major obstacles that the department encounters when trying to improve diversion rates?

I think the enca— I think the challenges that we encounter are, you know, pretty obvious. There's, I think, just general apathy around, you know, doing the right thing. And I think that's something that we've struggled with the most. There are much more solvable problems, which is giving people the tools to do the right thing, telling them how to do it. And we have focused a lot on those areas in the past, making sure that, for example, every apartment building out there has their required recycling receptacles in the required places, making sure that they have a brown bin and they're using the brown bin. That's sort of the first step. But, you know, actually changing behavior and getting people to stop and think about what should I

do with this thing that I want to throw away? Which bin does it go in? And why do— why should I do that? I think that's the more challenging area and that's somewhere that we have more work to do.

And you just mentioned the brown bins. Given that organics make up a third of our waste, do you think that the brown bins that we currently have are appropriately sized to capture all of the organics suitable for composting in a household?

So we have in the past given out free brown bins to both single-family homeowners all the way up to apartment buildings. That's not something that we currently do, because buildings are required to buy their trash cans. They should also be required to just buy their brown bins. You can go to Home Depot today and get department-branded NYC bins in various different sizes for your organics. You can have one, two, three, four and take whatever approach is right for you.

Can the agency provide a timeline for when it would be able to achieve 100 percent or close, you know, a suitable

number of organic— of diversions of organics from landfills and incinerators? Or is there an organics diversion rate that the agency anticipates that we can hold you accountable for in 10 years?
I think we would love to get to a capture rate that's similar to traditional curbside recyclables. I think if we were able to do that over the course of the next few years, that would be a win.
Great. And how specifically does DSNY plan to increase organics recycling access for NYCHA residents?

So we've done a lot of work with NYCHA to make sure that they have brown bins that residents can use. We have cited our orange bins, the smart composting bins at NYCHA developments in many cases, and done specific outreach to NYCHA residents to make sure that they, you know, can download the app on their phone, that they know how to use it, that they– that, you know, everyone who has a smart bin in their neighborhood knows what they're there for. I actually compost personally with a smart bin because I find it super easy to just drop it in on the way to daycare in the

morning. So that's been, I think, our number one approach. We also work with NYCHA a lot on the amount of yard waste that they generate. So things like leaves, grass clippings, and other plant material. They have actually an incredible amount of green space. And if we can capture the yard waste that they're generating, that can make a really big impact. And so we focused a lot on their leaves during leaf season, making sure that they're bagging them separately and that we're actually picking it up separately.

Curious, has there been any dedicated outreach to NYCHA residents about, you know, being a groundskeeper or a, you know, organics lead or a recycling lead? Is there any conversation or any programs that exist like that?

Nothing that I'm aware of that currently exists. I am just a week back into this, so, you know, I will dig into that more, and if there aren't programs like that, I'm happy to work with you to set them up. Oh, and we do have— Kate reminds me, a program that we set up a few years ago called the Clean Buildings Training, which is specifically focused on giving people the tools to

basically set up their building recyclables properly. So we do work with NYCHA staff to host that training. At the end of the training, everyone gets a certificate that I sign myself that, you know, certifies them as a trained clean buildings employee.

Okay, cool. I would love to see an expansion of these programs to really see NYCHA residents get a true workforce development program from DSNY with NYCHA residents. Something that I have seen in my own community is if you empower the local NYCHA residents with things to do, the other community members end up really falling behind, especially if you have your TA leaders or your presidents doing that. So if you can connect folks, you know, I think we can see an increase, hopefully, knock on wood, in diversion rates if we really start integrating local community. You have mentioned Rikers Island. Curious, outside of Rikers Island, are there any plans to construct additional composting facilities similar to Fresh Kills, and if so, would these facilities be designed to accept both commercial and residential organic food?

So right now we operate just the Staten Island Compost Facility,

which is next to the former Fresh Kills Landfill. We don't have sites identified at this time for additional food and yard waste composting facilities. We would love to work with City Council to identify where those could go. It's not particularly easy to site and permit a new facility, waste management facility. Even though these are compost sites, they are waste management facilities, and there are a lot of requirements under both the state regulations and local zoning that apply there. And so if we can work together to identify where those sites could be, we're happy to do so.

Great. And then one of the things that I have been very curious about and reading through the SWMP is, if I'm not mistaken, restaurants have a four percent organics diversion rate, which seems absolutely outrageous to me. Are there any initiatives understanding why the diversion rate is so low when it comes to restaurants? Are there any initiatives to increase that? And are there any plans that have seen either in New York or in other cities in the US or around the world that have been able to work with restaurants and really dive into the circular economy?

Yeah, so I think commercial waste zones first and foremost will have a big impact there, because one of the requirements is that carters charge less for composting and recycling than they charge for trash collection. So there's a direct financial incentive for businesses to separate more, both traditional recyclables and food waste. One of the things that I think has held us back here is that the sort of legal framework is very complicated. There are requirements around which restaurants are required to separate organic waste. It's a square footage requirement. It's not easy for restaurants to know, am I supposed to do it? Do I have to do it? Am I not required? So one of the things we'd love to work with the council on is just streamlining that and making it so that every food-related business has to separate their organic waste. We think that's a pretty straightforward thing to do, and you know, timing it around the rollout of commercial waste zones, I think would be the right way to go forward.
Luckily, I have my legislative director right in the front row, just taking copious amounts of notes.
We're happy to work with your office and with the Committee Counsel to get that moving.

And speaking about these partnerships, has the DSNY considered public-private partnerships to help construct composting facilities? And if so, can you describe the type and construct of partnerships demonstrating opportunities for success?

Yeah, so many of our recycling and composting facilities are public-private partnerships. They're either facilities on public land that are built by private entities like our Sunset Park MRF, or they're facilities that are operated by public— or by private entities like the Staten Island Compost Facility. So there's a lot of precedent there for public-private partnerships, and it's something that we are certainly dedicated to expanding. We also did just last Thursday, cut the ribbon on a new composting facility, more community scale. Although, you know, certainly larger than your average community garden compost facility. This is in Gowanus at the new Salt Lot in partnership with Big Reuse and Gowanus Canal

Conservancy. I think that model of sort of mid-scale compost facility, I think is great because it allows people to get hands-on with the material. They can see the food waste and the yard waste going in on one end. They can see the finished compost coming out the other end, and really participate in composting in real time. And so I think we would like to explore ways to expand that.

I have never heard something more Gowanus in my life. What specifically will DSNY do to ensure that our waste management practices do not intensify the burdens associated with biosolids derived from sewer sludge that is produced via the digestion processes?

So, I think first and foremost, DEP is responsible for the biosolids management program. The SWMP does account for biosolids. We are required to under the DEC regulations, but we did a lot of engagement with DEP, but they are the sort of lead there. So we just incorporated their planning and approach in the plan. Jen, anything else you want to say there?

I will say that that is one section that we updated post-first

draft, both based on public comment and input and also DEP's revisions to this section, as the Commissioner mentioned. Though, that portion of the plan was updated to reflect some of the concerns expressed through the comments, but also the changing regulatory landscape for that material.
Thank you. My last question in organics: if we do increase the organics, waste tonnage by 20 percent, how would this impact existing contract obligations and costs?

So I think, you know, as I said before, we have sufficient capacity to increase the amount of organics that we are diverting by a good share. You know, I will say just very bluntly that, you know, the organics processing is not cheaper than disposal. So, simply moving food waste from the trash stream into the organic stream doesn't in and of itself save money. I think as we expand the program and as we achieve greater and greater diversion, there could be some economies of scale that we generate there, and you know, to the extent that we can use city facilities to manage our organic waste, obviously that's something that can save us money.
Thank you, and I would like to welcome Council Member Hanif, and also turn the mic over.

Thank you, Chair, and welcome, Commissioner Anderson. It's really great to see you, and I'm super excited by the salt lot opening up and Big Reuse, Gowanus Canal Conservancy operating that composting facility. All good stuff. I want to continue the line of questioning around organics. How is the department ensuring accessibility of the program for seniors and people with disabilities?

So, you know, the program is today available citywide. Every single residential property in New York City has once a week curbside collection, and as we rolled the program out, we did offer free brown bins to every resident who wanted one. So we gave folks the opportunity to sort of request the bins, and then we delivered the bins ahead of the rollout of that program. So I think that's the sort of top thing that we've done. Our focus right now is on people who live in apartment buildings and making sure that their building management is giving them the opportunity to

participate, and if they are not, anyone can call 311. We'll send out outreach staff and if necessary enforcement.
And has there been anything more specific to ensuring that seniors and folks with disabilities have bin access, are compliant with their building?
We haven't had any specific programs focused on seniors, but I'm happy to work with you on what that could look like.
Got it. And then the same for, like, in terms of outreach to seniors and people with disabilities, would be very curious what the engagement has been.
Yeah, I think there's definite opportunity there to do outreach, particularly through our senior centers and older adult centers, but to my knowledge, we have not specifically done that at this time.

Okay, good to know. In my district, we partnered with Techfin, a nonprofit that collects laptops from corporations. They also collect desktop computers. They repair the machines and then distribute them to low-income

households. We distributed laptops to our adult literacy classes and would really love to know what opportunities are currently underway with the commercial sector to create a more circular economy for valuable materials like hardware, used hardware, rather than condemning materials to simple e-waste collection?

I think that's something that we would love to do more on. I think once we have commercial waste zones fully rolled out, we'll have a much better picture of the material that commercial businesses are actually generating. And we will have a much closer relationship with those businesses because we'll have only three carters per zone who are offering service rather than several dozen. So I think there's definitely a potential and a captive audience there, and we'd love to collaborate on expanding something like that.
And then does the department see an opportunity to expand commercial waste circularity from e-waste to furniture?

I think there is certainly a potential there. We, wherever possible, it's better to reuse durable goods than to just

recycle them. So, certainly we would want to work with the reuse entities like Goodwill, like Big Reuse and others to try to maximize the amount of material that is reusable that is getting reused.

And then on construction and demolition waste– so, the draft SWMP includes several proposals to increase reuse and recycling of construction and demolition waste, estimated at two million tons of material per year. Could you share if the department has considered comprehensive reform of this industry by setting rigorous standards for working conditions, safety, recycling, and community impacts?

So we— I mean, we certainly have considered it in the past. It's never been something that we've sort of put pen to paper on as far as drafting legislation. And, you know, I– my focus currently is on completing the implementation of commercial waste zones by the end of next year. After we get that done, I think we would be very interested in turning to the construction demolition collection and processing industry. You know, we do have for the first time ever, a number of initiatives in the SWMP around C&D material, and, you know,

we're— I think it's an area that we're excited to do more with. And yeah, I think more conversations to come, and we're happy to sit down with you and talk through what that could look like.
Wonderful, thank you.

Thank you so much. And thank you for bringing up C&D. I want to know– so C&D is responsible for approximately half of the city's overall waste production, and we know with the current admin, the former admin, and just the general housing crisis that we in— that we are in, it's all about building. And when you build, you're going to have construction and debris. And we just approved a brand new project in the South Bronx that's going to even bring more construction, construction everywhere. And so I would like to know– you know, even though it's regulated by the city's Business Integrity Commission, from the agency's perspective, can you describe some of the most effective ways to reduce C&D waste production? And what, if at all, will be the agency's role in trying to implement these programs?

Yeah, so I think, you know, there are– there are both builders and haulers out there right now that do a really good job of sustainable deconstruction and recycling of construction demolition waste. There's a C&D processing facility/material recovery facility in Brooklyn that I think is certainly at the top of the pack here in New York City. There are also many facilities that, you know, simply take in material. They pull out, you know, whatever metal products that they can, and a lot of the rest just goes to landfill. That's certainly not what we want to see. But we don't have a great regulatory framework at this moment around, you know, capturing more of the material that can be recycled. So I think that's something that we are sort of starting to look at in this SWMP and will continue to refine as we move to implementation.

C&D was left out— was exempt from Local Law 199. I'm curious as to the appetite to bring it into compliance. If not, or were there specific policy reasons from the agency's perspective in which leaving C&D out of 199 is for a particular reason?

Yeah, I think that the focus of Local Law 199 was on the sort of curbside collection, curbside and containerized collection of waste generated inside of businesses. It's a much more predictable stream because those businesses are open all year long. They're putting out waste several times a week. With construction demolition debris, it's a much more sort of itinerant type of generation where, you know, you may have a building that's going up for a few months or a few years in one location, and then that generation stops once the building's done. There's no more construction demolition waste. So, the sort of zoned model didn't necessarily apply as easily to the construction industry. But it's something that we're happy to dig into more with you. I will say because it's a place that has so much emphasis from– both from the mayor's office and from the City Council as far as building affordably. We want to be very careful about introducing new regulations that increase the cost of construction. And so I think that's something that we will be very attuned to as we explore these options going forward.

Appreciate it. I think a lot of the costs are associated more on the maintenance and the insurance cost for buildings, not necessarily the construction piece. And speaking of construction a lot of what we're trying to do with C&D is talking about how we recycle and reuse materials. I'm curious, has there been any research, or if you can share with us the research on the use of these recycled materials and their lifespan as opposed to other materials, how they shape up compared to other building materials, if you have those? I know you're not DOB. So I'm very aware of the limitations you might have. But as we're looking at these reuse and recycle rates, have we been looking at the data further before we, you know, move full steam ahead in doing all of these, you know, great reuse and recycle ideas? But, will that make our buildings worse off?

Yeah. So I know we've participated in industry working groups around a couple different products specifically. I know we've done some work around concrete. We've also done some work around gypsum wallboard, and that's something that Kate and her team have been involved

in. Kate, I don't know if there's anything specific you want to add there. But that's, I think, an area that the industry is really putting a lot of work into. We are, you know, more a stakeholder there rather than the primary convener. But, you know, certainly hear the point you're making, and we'll take that into account. We also have a waste characterization study for the commercial waste industry that is–
[interposing] My next question.
that is currently scheduled for 2032.
We have an update where we are on that? Have you guys started the process yet, or you just—

[interposing] We have not. We have a residential waste characterization study in between that's due in 2028, so that will be our first focus, and then we'll shift to the commercial study after that, but that will look at both the commercial waste zones commercial waste as well as the construction demolition waste.
Thank you so much. I would like to now turn it over to Council Member Chanel Thomas-Henry.

Thank you, Chair. How are you doing today? I have a couple of questions surrounding illegal dumping. Are there any new ways of catching individuals? I know you have the cameras and you can catch the license plates, but in my district particularly, we have a lot of dumping where individuals are literally— they may not be driving the car, they're taking it from their homes and just dropping them in places. Is there any way to crack down on those type of offenders? And how successful has the program been with capturing the license plates?

Yeah, so the illegal dumping camera program, which largely ramped up under my predecessor, Jesse Tish in 2022, has been very successful. I don't have the camera numbers in front of me, but, you know, we have a couple hundred cameras across the city. We have really increased the amount of enforcement that we're able to do on illegal dumping. We also worked with you all in the City Council to increase the penalties for illegal

dumping, which I think has had a big impact on encouraging folks not to do it in the first place. So I think there's a lot of good news there, and we're happy to share more with you on how that's gone. One of the things that we're looking at now is how do we make the cameras more adaptable? Because right now, you know, you spend a lot of money, you put a camera up in one place, once that camera is there and people know it's there, they're going to avoid it. So we're looking at ways that we can use mobile cameras, and you know, really increase the sort of breadth of that program without spending a lot more money. Yeah, 334 cameras citywide. As far as the other kind of dumping, which we technically refer to as improper disposal because it's not done with the vehicle, it doesn't have the higher $4,000 penalty, you know, that is very challenging for us to enforce, because we either have to see someone doing it or we have to very manually open up the bags, see if there's any identifying information inside, like a piece of mail or an Amazon box or something like that. We certainly do that, and do write tickets based on that, but it is much more laborious than the illegal dumping cameras.

So with the illegal dumping award program, are individuals who actually catch people, be it the individuals who may not be in a vehicle, are they able to testify and do the affidavit if there is no vehicle involved?
So if there's no vehicle involved, currently no.
Okay.

But that's something that I would love to expand both the affidavit program for illegal dumping from vehicles as well as other citizen enforcement programs. I think there's a great model at DEP that has been very successful on commercial idling that I'd love to explore how we could bring that into the sanitation sector.

Okay. And last question– with the fine, like I know with the award program, half the fine would go to the person who helps– who captures it. Currently when the cameras catch someone, does half— do half the award go into more sanitation pickups in that particular district or additional cleanups, or how is the– how

are the funds dispersed? Do they go into a general pot?
Yeah. So right now those fines that are paid are going into the general fund.
Okay.

So they're not being reinvested specifically in the areas that have the cameras, but it's something that I think we would love to have a conversation with you about and with OMB about how we could potentially stand something like that up.
Thank you.
Thank you so much. And I'd like to turn it over back again to Council Member Zhuang.

Thank you, Chair and Commissioner, in my district I have a lot of seniors coming to my office saying they are not able to go to buy those garbage bins city required. And then they order online last year, they still never get it. In the same time, they get tickets. And my office helped them to find those garbage bins in Home Depot, but they don't deliver. Is any– city has any

program to help those seniors, probably some disabled people too, with those needs? My office actually had a constituent service person went to the store with the constituent, bought that thing, bring to his home. For our office to do that for every single constituent, that's impossible. Is Sanitation has any program to help those people?

Yeah, so first, I know prior to when I started, there were some issues with the NYC bins and with the contractor making deliveries that they were required to. I'm happy to say that every single order that was placed before the online orders were suspended last fall has been made as of March 30th of this year. So all of those orders have been fulfilled. The new model going forward is that they are available at retail at Home Depot. We're also happy to work with you.
They don't deliver.

I'm going to get there in one second. We're also happy to work with you if there are other community hardware stores or other facilities that want to sell the bins, we're happy to make them available through those retailers.

And then the last thing is they are available via delivery through online delivery partners that Home Depot has partnered with, things like Uber and Instacart, and I think there's a third one. I, you know, I'm on day eight here, and you know, have not been super pleased by how this program has sort of evolved over the last six months, and so would be happy to dig in with you on if there are specific ways that we can make bins available to your community members, particularly seniors and people with disabilities.
Yeah, seniors, probably they need the most. And also for Reso 125, what's the cost of this? And can this– can this institution shoulder it for Reso 125?
We don't have a specific cost for the resolution, but you know, I'm sure we'd be happy to work with CUNY and SUNY on what that cost would look like.
Okay, because, I think it's a good idea, but I worry the cost is too big. And also for—

[interposing] Yeah, and I'll just say that we already have curbside

collection in every neighborhood in New York City so that there isn't really a substantial cost for sanitation to provide the service, but there would be some cost on the CUNY and SUNY side just as far as making sure that they're— that they have the bins that they need, that they have the training that they need in order to be able to separate properly.

So in the— before we talk about the West Transfer Station, we will have the commercial waste transfer– waste come to, like, all the waste transfer stations, especially the one near me. What's the measurement you guys have to make sure those commercial trucks follow rules? And how– if they don't follow the rule, what's the penalty there? How the community monitor that?

Yeah, so, as I mentioned before, we do not have explicit plans today to accept commercial waste at the MTSs. It's something that we are going to start exploring once Commercial Waste Zones is fully rolled out at the end of next year, and as we explore what that could look like, we're happy to work with you and other community stakeholders to do that in a way that works for the community. I will say that under Commercial

Waste Zones, we have an incredible amount of regulatory authority over the private haulers. We actually receive their, like, minute-by-minute GPS pings. We know where all of their trucks are at every time of the day. We can really crack down on unsafe driving, crack down on emissions, crack down on failure to separate recyclables and all kinds of things that previously it's been very difficult for the city to enforce. And so I think that's the real promise of the commercial waste zones program and one that I'm excited to realize at the end of next year.
Will that increase the cost for small business owners?

We've actually seen that the rates have not gone up as a result of the implementation of commercial waste zones and in some cases have actually decreased because we're implement— implementing a system that is incredibly efficient with only three carters operating in each zone. The carters can have much more efficient routes and operations. And so they're passing along those savings to businesses.
Thank you.
